**H1 doesn't hold: the markdown is a mechanical clearance price on discontinued equipment sold from branch stock, not a discount anyone chooses. The actionable leak is that two discontinued waves keep being restocked at standard cost and sold off the 42% ladder (-2.79M gross profit in 2025)**

The 2015 and 2023 discontinuation waves are still bought in at standard cost and sold from branch stock at the 0.42 cap. Marked-down stock lines lost -767,211 and -2,022,425 of gross profit in 2025, -2,789,637 together, so stopping restocking would avoid up to about 2.79M a year if that demand simply goes away. Confidence is medium. Next step: ask purchasing why these two waves are still restocked when the 2025 wave's stock buys fell from 10,326 to 582 units, pilot a stop at a few branches against branches that keep restocking, cost the 3,571 on-hand 2025-wave units at the cap against vendor return at 0.80 of standard cost, and have markdown reporting count only stock-filled lines.

**On hand-keyed orders a fixed share of shipped lines never reaches an invoice: about $285K a year at order price ($72K gross margin), worst at the counter, never billed later. The part still worth chasing is the recent tail of about $271K**

0.194% of shipped lines, all from counter, email and phone orders (counter worst at 1.124%), never reached an invoice, even though the goods left and were not billed anywhere else. That is 285,468.20 a year at order price, or 71,523.61 a year of gross margin, and confidence is high. Next step: give accounting the 490 lines (271,314.82, 408 customers) from the last 252 operating days, starting with the 156 lines (90,763.66) from the last 85, to confirm and back-bill where terms allow; add a daily report of shipped lines with no invoice line; and block credit memos against lines never invoiced.

**Overdue receivables sit in a persistent 'very slow' tier: customers flagged on 2016-19 data alone (152 accounts, 5.3% of 2020-24 billing) held 29.0% of the 2020-24 overdue balance. No recorded attribute explains the tier, including terms and credit limits.**

Bringing those 152 accounts to prompt lateness would have released 786,932 of receivables, worth 62,955 a year at an assumed 8% (range 30,760 to 136,567 a year), before any sales lost to tighter collections. Confidence is medium, because the tiers may reflect how the records were generated rather than real payer behaviour. Next step: review the very slow list with credit/AR for disputes or standing arrangements, then randomise half to collection calls at due_day + 5 with half as a control, rather than tightening terms across the board.

Several things were checked and found not to hold. The markdown is not a rep, branch or customer discount. It follows a fixed ladder of 0.021 per month capped at 0.42, it cuts price only on stock-filled lines, and it shows no lift in quote wins (difference-in-differences -0.004). Most of the 13.26M "markdown dollars" is a reporting overstatement, not money given away. The challenger's higher 4.78M saving is not supported, and the vendor credits are returns at 80% of cost, not rebates. The missing invoice lines are not a linkage error, and they are not any person's fault: rep-level counts match chance across all 48 inside reps. Slow payment is not bad debt, since every 2016-24 invoice was paid in full. Terms, credit limits, size, tenure, trade and branch don't explain who pays late, and rep variation is close to chance.

The records can't answer the following. They can't show how much 42%-off stock demand would move to special orders if restocking stopped. They can't show what "discontinued" means in practice, since SKUs flagged in 2015 are still bought every year. They don't show which orders special POs serve, or what triggers stock POs on discontinued SKUs. They can't show whether any unbilled sales were collected outside the ERP, why lines drop, how much of the recent tail is recoverable, or whether the 234 special-order lines physically shipped. They don't explain why the very slow accounts pay late, whether credit holds or limits are enforced, whether early-pay discounts or late fees exist, or how many sales tighter collections would cost.
